name: Surface Splatting and Lighting
text:
# Surface Splatting and Lighting


## Overview
Surface Splatting and Lighting is a family of rendering techniques that convert unstructured point clouds into continuous, shaded surfaces by projecting points as splats into a rendering pipeline [S2, unofficial]. It solves sparse dot cloud aliasing and transparency artifacts by assigning each point sample an extent drawn as a small oriented primitive (a splat) carrying a radially decreasing [reconstruction kernel](#8724-splat-kernels-and-footprints.md) [S2, unofficial]. It differs from its parent [EWA Splatting](1069-ewa-splatting.md) by using screen-aligned spherical impostors with isotropic linear falloff rather than anisotropic, correctly band-limited EWA footprints, trading accurate filtering for a formulation that requires no per-point normals or radii [S2, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The family shares the core mechanism of treating each point sample as a local surface patch that is rasterized as a primitive (typically a point sprite or quadrilateral) to cover the area where the underlying surface is expected to exist. The rendering pipeline accumulates surface attributes (color, normal, depth) from overlapping splats to reconstruct a continuous signal. Lighting is applied either during the accumulation pass (if normals are available per-splat) or in a deferred screen-space pass using the accumulated normal buffer.

## Subtopics

### [Deferred Surface Splatting](1072-deferred-surface-splatting.md)
[Deferred Surface Splatting](#1072-deferred-surface-splatting.md) is a rendering technique that converts unstructured point clouds into continuous, shaded surfaces by projecting points as splats into a deferred rendering pipeline. It solves sparse dot cloud aliasing and transparency artifacts by assigning each point sample an extent drawn as a small oriented primitive (a splat) carrying a radially decreasing reconstruction kernel. It differs from its parent [EWA Splatting](1069-ewa-splatting.md) by using screen-aligned spherical impostors with isotropic linear falloff rather than anisotropic, correctly band-limited EWA footprints, trading accurate filtering for a formulation that requires no per-point normals or radii. It differs from siblings like [Phong Splatting](2802-phong-splatting.md) by deferring the [lighting calculation](#2056-lighting-models.md) to a final screen-space pass, allowing multiple light sources to be applied efficiently without re-projecting geometry [G].

### [Phong Splatting](2802-phong-splatting.md)
[Phong Splatting](#2802-phong-splatting.md) is a surface [splatting](#23-splatting.md) technique that assigns a linearly varying normal field to each elliptical splat, enabling per-pixel [Phong shading](#1853-phong-shading.md) without surface connectivity. It solves the piecewise constant shading artifacts of standard point-based rendering by providing smooth, Phong-like shading quality on modern GPUs. Unlike its sibling [EWA Splatting](1069-ewa-splatting.md), which uses a simplified isotropic kernel, Phong Splatting uses elliptical splats with projectively correct per-pixel parameterization, trading the simplicity of isotropic filtering for superior visual quality and exact depth values.

### EWA Surface Splatting
**Definition:** A method where EWA volume splats reduce to surface splats suitable for high-quality iso-surface rendering by flattening the [3D Gaussian kernel](#6228-primitive-geometry-and-distribution.md) along the volume gradient [S1, unofficial].
**Step:** For each point in object-space, quadrilaterals texture-mapped with a Gaussian texture are deformed to result in the correct screen-space EWA splat after projection [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of EWA surface splats was derived by Ren et al. [Ren et al. 2002] as an object-space formulation of EWA volume splats, describing an efficient implementation on graphics hardware [S1, unofficial]. The technique involves deforming quadrilaterals texture-mapped with a Gaussian texture to result in the correct screen-space EWA splat after projection [S1, unofficial]. This approach allows for high-quality iso-surface rendering by flattening the 3D Gaussian kernel along the volume gradient [S1, unofficial].
